children.value: Continuous conduction at the 0.1 A minimum would need an inductor of that size that can also carry the full load current. The sheet says an inductor like that is not readily available. Page 12 of the LTC3891 datasheet says the controller allows the inductor current to go discontinuous and uses high-efficiency Burst Mode, so the inductor can be chosen for the desired ripple, with the peak flux kept below saturation.
The page 16 estimate, aimed at 30% of the 7.5 A short-circuit peak and the 46 V input, prints 15.77 µH. A 20% margin for tolerance brings that to 18.92 µH. The value selected in the sheet is 22 µH.

With the 22 µH inductor, the textbook ripple at nominal duty is 1.658 A peak to peak, and half of that is 0.829 A. The application-note form, using the 56 V input and the minimum duty, prints 1.714 A peak to peak, and half of that is 0.857 A.
The peak current uses that second ripple:

children.html: Ipeak,nom=5 A+1.714 A2=5.857 AI_{peak,nom} = 5\,\mathrm{A} + \frac{1.714\,\mathrm{A}}{2} = 5.857\,\mathrm{A}Ipeak,nom​=5A+21.714A​=5.857A

children.value: Page 21 of the LTC3891 datasheet gives a minimum on time of 95 ns. Divided by the 4.0 µs period, the short-circuit duty is 0.02375. The ripple at 56 V and 22 µH is then 0.236 A peak to peak.
The earlier ripple guess was 1.75 A. The sheet’s note is that the guess is larger than this calculated short-circuit ripple, so the margin to saturation is enough and no adjustment is needed.
